title: How to Report Project Status as an Engineering Leader
author: Karol Wojciszko
summary: Drawing on a story from a pharma-industry engineering role, the author describes how a 10-chart, 20-metric status presentation left executives nodding blankly because they had no framework to interpret Monte Carlo simulations or variance charts. His manager's fix was radical simplification: replace the charts with a green/yellow/red signal and one or two sentences. The piece argues for a sharp distinction between tracking (the leader's private, comprehensive understanding of project health) and reporting (a distilled read tailored to an audience that doesn't share the leader's context). It closes with concrete disciplines: lead with the assessment rather than the evidence, make asks explicit, favor frequent short updates over rare comprehensive ones, and never let a stakeholder learn bad news for the first time in a group setting.
points: Distinguish "tracking" (your own private, comprehensive model of project health) from "reporting" (a distilled signal for stakeholders who don't share your context).
A three-color (green/yellow/red) signal system, sent in frequent short updates, communicates project health better than detailed chart-based presentations executives can't parse.
Yellow and red updates should always include a specific ask or plan; red news should reach the affected person privately before it appears in a group setting.
Increasing update frequency while reducing length beats a comprehensive report delivered rarely, because stakeholders need "current," not "comprehensive."
quotes: They didn't understand Monte Carlo simulations, they didn't know how to read variance charts - so they couldn't tell if the project was fine or falling apart.
My manager's suggestion: ditch the charts. Replace everything with one of three signals - green, yellow, or red emoji. That's it.
That question forced me to think harder about something I hadn't fully worked out before: what does it actually mean to assess project health?
The distinction that changed everything for me: you track for yourself, you report for your audience.
Lead with the assessment, not the evidence. What's your honest read on where things stand? Say that first. The supporting detail is optional - they'll ask if they want it.

The data was for me - to stay oriented, to catch things early, to know when I was about to have a real problem. The update was for them - to give them a clear read on where we stood and what, if anything, they needed to do.
